Apple___Apple_scab.cause: Fungal infection by Venturia inaequalis favored by cool, wet spring weather.
Apple___Apple_scab.treatment: Rake and destroy infected leaves. Apply appropriate fungicides during the budding stage to prevent infection.
Apple___Apple_scab.simple_explanation: This disease causes dark, crusty spots on apple leaves and fruit. It mostly spreads during cool, rainy weather.
Apple___Apple_scab.prevention: Always clear fallen leaves around the tree to stop the spread. Prune branches so more sunlight and wind can dry the leaves.

Apple___Black_rot.cause: Fungal pathogen Botryosphaeria obtusa that enters through wounds and dead tissue.
Apple___Black_rot.treatment: Prune out dead or diseased wood. Apply a preventative fungicidal spray schedule starting early in the season.
Apple___Black_rot.simple_explanation: Black rot makes leaves turn yellow and creates dark, rotting spots on apples. It starts when the tree has been cut or injured.
Apple___Black_rot.prevention: Cut away and burn any dead or sick branches immediately. Be careful not to damage the tree bark when working around it.

Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.cause: Fungal infection by Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae relying on both apple and cedar trees to complete its life cycle.
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.treatment: Remove nearby cedar/juniper hosts if possible. Apply preventative fungicidal sprays when apple blossoms open.
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.simple_explanation: This creates bright orange spots on your apple leaves. It strangely needs a nearby cedar or juniper tree to survive.
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.prevention: If possible, do not plant apple trees near cedar trees. Spray the tree early in the spring before the blossoms fully open.

Apple___healthy.cause: Optimal environmental conditions and successful pathogen prevention.
Apple___healthy.treatment: No treatment needed. Continue routine watering, pruning, and monitoring.
Apple___healthy.simple_explanation: Your apple tree looks perfectly healthy and free from diseases!
Apple___healthy.prevention: Keep doing a great job! Maintain regular watering, fertilizing, and seasonal pruning.

Blueberry___healthy.cause: Optimal soil acidity (pH 4.5-5.5) and pathogen-free environment.
Blueberry___healthy.treatment: No treatment needed. Maintain optimal soil pH and employ general good agricultural practices.
Blueberry___healthy.simple_explanation: Your blueberry plant is completely healthy!
Blueberry___healthy.prevention: Blueberries love acidic soil. Continue applying acidic mulch like pine needles to keep the soil healthy.

Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.cause: Fungal disease (Podosphaera clandestina) favored by high humidity and dry weather.
Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.treatment: Apply sulfur or potassium bicarbonate sprays. Ensure good air circulation by regular pruning.
Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.simple_explanation: This looks like a white, powdery dust covering the cherry leaves. It happens when it is humid but not raining.
Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.prevention: Prune your cherry tree to let more air flow through the branches. Don't water the tree from the top to prevent wet leaves.

Cherry_(including_sour)___healthy.cause: Proper care and resistance to local pathogens.
Cherry_(including_sour)___healthy.treatment: No treatment needed. Ensure appropriate watering and sunlight.
Cherry_(including_sour)___healthy.simple_explanation: The cherry plant is strong and healthy!
Cherry_(including_sour)___healthy.prevention: Continue standard care. Water deeply when it's dry and cut off any dead wood during winter.

Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.cause: Fungal pathogen Cercospora zeae-maydis thriving in prolonged high humidity and overcast conditions.
Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.treatment: Use resistant hybrids. Rotate crops and manage crop residue to reduce fungal overwintering. Apply fungicides if necessary.
Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.simple_explanation: This causes rectangular grey or brown spots on corn leaves, eventually killing the leaf. It spreads fast in wet, cloudy weather.
Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.prevention: Plant corn seeds that are resistant to spots. Do not plant corn in the exact same field two years in a row.

Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.cause: Fungi Puccinia sorghi carried by wind from warmer areas, progressing in cool, humid temperatures.
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.treatment: Use rust-resistant hybrids. Early foliar fungicide application can reduce severity if detected early.
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.simple_explanation: You'll see dark, reddish-brown powdery bumps on both sides of the corn leaves. Wind brings this rust to the farm.
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.prevention: The best defense is buying rust-resistant corn seed. Check your fields often so you can spray early if you see rusty powder.

Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.cause: Fungal disease caused by Exserohilum turcicum under moderate temperatures and heavy dew/humidity.
Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.treatment: Plant resistant corn hybrids. Till crop residue to limit spore survival and use crop rotation.
Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.simple_explanation: This creates large, cigar-shaped grey spots on the corn leaves. It loves places with heavy morning dew.
Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.prevention: Plow any leftover corn stalks deep into the dirt after harvest so the disease can't survive the winter. Plant resistant seed types.

Corn_(maize)___healthy.cause: Sufficient nutrients and lack of pest/pathogen pressure.
Corn_(maize)___healthy.treatment: No treatment needed. Maintain good fertilization and watering regimens.
Corn_(maize)___healthy.simple_explanation: Your corn looks green and perfectly healthy!
Corn_(maize)___healthy.prevention: Keep an eye on water levels and make sure the soil has enough fertilizer.

Grape___Black_rot.cause: Fungal infection Guignardia bidwellii affecting leaves and rotting the grapes, favored by warm, moist weather.
Grape___Black_rot.treatment: Remove infected mummies from vines. Ensure heavy canopy management for airflow, and apply protective fungicides.
Grape___Black_rot.simple_explanation: Leaves show small brown spots with dark rings, and the grapes turn black and shrivel up like hard raisins.
Grape___Black_rot.prevention: Pick off and burn any dead, shriveled grapes from the vine. Trim grapevines heavily so the wind dries them out fast after rain.

Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).cause: A complex of fungi attacking the vine's wood, severely limiting sap and nutrient transport.
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).treatment: Prune out infected wood down to healthy tissue. Disinfect pruning tools to prevent spreading. No chemical cure exists once established.
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).simple_explanation: This is a serious disease inside the wood of the vine. Leaves turn yellow between the veins, and grapes get dark measles-like spots.
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).prevention: Always clean your cutting tools with bleach or alcohol between plants. Cut off and burn woody parts that show dark spots inside.

Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.cause: Fungus Pseudocercospora vitis spread by rain splash and wind.
Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.treatment: Remove and burn fallen leaves. Treat with preventative copper-based fungicides if recurring annually.
Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.simple_explanation: This causes large, red or brown dead patches across the grape leaves. Rain splashes it from bottom leaves upwards.
Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.prevention: Keep the ground under the vines completely clear of old leaves. Spraying with organic copper treatments can block the disease.

Grape___healthy.cause: Appropriate canopy management and pest-free vines.
Grape___healthy.treatment: No treatment needed. Continue standard vineyard maintenance operations.
Grape___healthy.simple_explanation: Your grape vine is completely healthy and growing well!
Grape___healthy.prevention: Provide good sunlight, keep weeds low, and prune vines in the winter for a good harvest.

Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).cause: Bacterial disease spread by the Asian citrus psyllid insect.
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).treatment: Currently incurable. Remove and destroy infected trees immediately to prevent spread. Control the psyllid insect populations.
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).simple_explanation: This is a deadly citrus disease that causes yellow, blotchy leaves and stops oranges from turning orange. It is spread by a tiny bug.
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).prevention: There is no cure. You must chop down and burn the tree immediately so it doesn't infect your other citrus trees.

Peach___Bacterial_spot.cause: Bacterium Xanthomonas campestris pv. pruni spread by rain splash on wet leaves.
Peach___Bacterial_spot.treatment: Plant resistant varieties. Use copper or oxytetracycline sprays in early spring as a preventative measure.
Peach___Bacterial_spot.simple_explanation: Leaves get tiny purple or black spots, and holes start popping out as the leaf tries to drop the sick parts.
Peach___Bacterial_spot.prevention: Try not to get leaves wet when watering. Buy peach trees that are known to fight off leaf spots.

Peach___healthy.cause: Good preventative care and absence of pathogens.
Peach___healthy.treatment: No treatment needed. Keep regular pruning schedules to promote airflow.
Peach___healthy.simple_explanation: Your peach tree is very healthy!
Peach___healthy.prevention: Keep the area around the base clean, and trim branches that cross each other so sunlight can enter.

Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.cause: Bacterium Xanthomonas campestris favored by high moisture and temperatures.
Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.treatment: Avoid overhead watering. Apply copper-based bactericides early. Rotate crops and remove infected plants.
Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.simple_explanation: This creates small, dark, water-soaked spots on the pepper leaves and the peppers themselves. Hot, wet weather makes it worse.
Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.prevention: Water your peppers at the base near the dirt, never spray water over the top. Plant your peppers in a different spot next year.

Pepper,_bell___healthy.cause: Well-drained soil and healthy environmental conditions.
Pepper,_bell___healthy.treatment: No treatment needed. Keep consistent soil moisture.
Pepper,_bell___healthy.simple_explanation: Your bell pepper plant is totally healthy!
Pepper,_bell___healthy.prevention: Keep watering the dirt directly and keep weeds pulled so the plant has no competition.

Potato___Early_blight.cause: Fungus Alternaria solani affecting older leaves first during warm, alternating wet-and-dry weather.
Potato___Early_blight.treatment: Apply protectant fungicides like chlorothalonil. Practice a 3-year crop rotation.
Potato___Early_blight.simple_explanation: Early blight forms dark rings on older, lower potato leaves that look like a bullseye target.
Potato___Early_blight.prevention: Keep a thick layer of mulch on the ground to stop dirt splashing on the leaves. Wait 3 years before planting potatoes in the same dirt.

Potato___Late_blight.cause: Water mold Phytophthora infestans (the pathogen of the Irish Potato Famine), thriving in cool, consistently wet conditions.
Potato___Late_blight.treatment: Requires aggressive fungicidal sprays (e.g. copper formulations). Destroy infected plants and tubers immediately.
Potato___Late_blight.simple_explanation: This is highly dangerous. It causes large, dark, rotting spots on leaves and potatoes very fast. Whole crops can die in days.
Potato___Late_blight.prevention: Plant certified disease-free potatoes. If you see late blight, you must pull up and burn the plant far away from the farm.

Potato___healthy.cause: Successful prevention of soil-borne and airborne pathogens.
Potato___healthy.treatment: No treatment needed. Store harvested potatoes in cool, dry conditions.
Potato___healthy.simple_explanation: Your potato leaves look completely healthy!
Potato___healthy.prevention: Ensure potatoes are planted in soil that drains well. Never leave them sitting in muddy water.

Raspberry___healthy.cause: Adequate sunlight and good soil drainage.
Raspberry___healthy.treatment: No treatment needed. Thin canes in winter to ensure good spring airflow.
Raspberry___healthy.simple_explanation: The raspberry plant is perfectly healthy!
Raspberry___healthy.prevention: Prune away dead, grey canes in the winter so the new green stems have room to grow.

Soybean___healthy.cause: Optimized nitrogen fixation and pest control.
Soybean___healthy.treatment: No treatment needed. Monitor periodically for pests.
Soybean___healthy.simple_explanation: Your soybean crop looks green and has no sign of disease!
Soybean___healthy.prevention: Check under the leaves every few weeks for bugs, but otherwise, they are doing great.

Squash___Powdery_mildew.cause: Fungal species thriving in high humidity, even without direct rainfall, affecting older leaves.
Squash___Powdery_mildew.treatment: Apply sulfur or neem oil early. Ensure sufficient spacing between vines for optimal air circulation.
Squash___Powdery_mildew.simple_explanation: Older squash leaves get covered in a white powder like flour. This blocks sunlight and kills the leaf.
Squash___Powdery_mildew.prevention: Plant squash far apart so air can quickly dry out. Keep leaves dry by watering near the roots only.

Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.cause: Fungus Diplocarpon earlianum which infects leaves via rain droplets.
Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.treatment: Remove infected foliage. Keep the foliage as dry as possible using drip irrigation instead of overhead sprinklers.
Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.simple_explanation: Strawberry leaves show dark purple blotches, making the leaves look like they have been scorched by fire.
Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.prevention: Only run your water hoses along the dirt. Spacing plants so they aren't touching will drastically reduce the risk.

Strawberry___healthy.cause: Good field sanitation and weather conditions.
Strawberry___healthy.treatment: No treatment needed. Maintain clean straw mulch layers to prevent soil splashing.
Strawberry___healthy.simple_explanation: Your strawberry patch is completely healthy!
Strawberry___healthy.prevention: Put a nice layer of straw mulch under the berries to keep them off the wet dirt so they don't rot.

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.cause: Seed-borne or splash-spread bacterial infection (Xanthomonas) degrading foliage and fruit.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.treatment: Use disease-free seeds. Apply copper bactericides. Remove infected debris and avoid overhead watering.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.simple_explanation: Tomato leaves get many small, black or brown crusty spots. It can ruin tomatoes quickly in wet weather.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.prevention: Always use clean, fresh seeds. Avoid getting the leaves wet because water carries the bacteria.

Tomato___Early_blight.cause: Alternaria solani fungus creating 'bullseye' target spots on lower leaves.
Tomato___Early_blight.treatment: Remove affected lower leaves immediately. Prevent soil splash with thick mulch. Use preventative fungicides.
Tomato___Early_blight.simple_explanation: Like potatoes, lower tomato leaves get dark spots shaped like targets, which slowly makes leaves turn yellow and die.
Tomato___Early_blight.prevention: Pick off any sick lower leaves as soon as you see them, and use a straw cover on the ground to stop splashing.

Tomato___Late_blight.cause: Aggressive infection by Phytophthora infestans spreading rapidly in cool, wet environments.
Tomato___Late_blight.treatment: Apply copper-based fungicides proactively. Once severe, the plant must be removed and destroyed (do not compost).
Tomato___Late_blight.simple_explanation: Rapidly spreading dark, greasy-looking spots appear on leaves, and an ugly rot takes over the tomatoes.
Tomato___Late_blight.prevention: If you catch it, it's often too late. Destroy the plant. Never compost infected tomatoes; bury them or burn them.

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.cause: Passalora fulva fungus that aggressively develops under high relative humidity (especially in greenhouses).
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.treatment: Improve airflow and reduce relative humidity. Apply appropriate preventative fungicides before symptom onset.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.simple_explanation: Yellow spots appear on the top of leaves, while a fuzzy green/brown mold grows underneath. Mostly a problem in greenhouses.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.prevention: Space your tomato plants far apart and keep fans on or windows open if in a greenhouse so humidity drops.

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.cause: Fungus Septoria lycopersici which causes numerous small circular spots, often splashing up from the soil.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.treatment: Apply mulch to stop soil-borne spores from splashing onto leaves. Use organic or heavy-duty fungicidal sprays.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.simple_explanation: You'll see lots of tiny spots with grey centers and dark edges. They eat the leaf until it dies and falls off.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.prevention: Placing cardboard or straw over the dirt stops this particular fungus from bouncing up onto your bottom leaves.

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.cause: Microscopic arachnids spinning webs and sucking plant sap, thriving in hot, dry conditions.
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.treatment: Wash off with strong water streams. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil targeting the undersides of leaves.
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.simple_explanation: Tiny, fast-moving red or black dots start sucking the juice out of your leaves, leaving a sandy-looking web behind.
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.prevention: Spray them off with a hard blast of water every day. If that fails, using safe Neem Oil on the leaves will stop them.

Tomato___Target_Spot.cause: Corynespora cassiicola fungus flourishing in prolonged periods of high humidity.
Tomato___Target_Spot.treatment: Increase air circulation through staking and pruning. Apply fungicides as recommended.
Tomato___Target_Spot.simple_explanation: Very similar to early blight, it shows up as brown circles. The centers often crack or fall out leaving holes.
Tomato___Target_Spot.prevention: Stake your tomatoes up tall so they don't drag on the dirt. Cut away weak branches to let air dry out the center of the plant.

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.cause: Devastating viral infection transmitted by the Silverleaf Whitefly.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.treatment: No cure for the virus. Manage whitefly populations aggressively using insecticidal soaps, oils, or predatory insects.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.simple_explanation: The top leaves of your tomato turn yellow and curl upwards tightly into extreme shapes, and growth stops.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.prevention: The disease is injected by tiny whiteflies. Killing or trapping whiteflies early is the only way to save nearby crops.

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.cause: Highly contagious virus transmitted manually via tools, hands, and clothing (often related to tobacco use).
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.treatment: No cure. Destroy infected plants immediately. Disinfect tools, wash hands thoroughly with soap, and do not smoke near tomatoes.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.simple_explanation: Leaves become thin, stringy, and show weird yellow-green patterns. It stunts the plant permanently.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.prevention: Wash your hands closely before touching plants, and do not smoke nearby (tobacco smoke carries the mosaic virus to tomatoes).

Tomato___healthy.cause: Consistent moisture, sufficient calcium levels, and robust pest prevention.
Tomato___healthy.treatment: No treatment needed. Keep up with pruning to allow sunlight penetration.
Tomato___healthy.simple_explanation: Your tomato plant looks super green, strong, and ready to produce fruit!
Tomato___healthy.prevention: Don't change your farming habits! Keep watering steadily and tie them up well so they support heavy fruit.
